# Installing and Setting Up Docker

Docker lets you run software in a small, isolated environment called a **container**. A container can include a particular version of R, packages, and system libraries, which helps make an analysis reproducible across computers.

Docker is optional for the basic R onboarding lessons. You should use it when your instructor, project, or lab instructions specifically ask you to.

## Learning Objectives

After completing this lesson, you should be able to:

- Explain the difference between an image and a container.
- Install Docker Desktop on Mac or Windows.
- Check that Docker is running.
- Run a simple R container.
- Make a local project folder available inside a container.

## Important Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Docker Desktop** | The application that runs Docker on Mac and Windows. |
| **Image** | A packaged template used to create containers. |
| **Container** | A running instance of an image. |
| **Registry** | A service that stores and shares images, such as Docker Hub. |
| **Volume or bind mount** | A way to make files persist or share a local folder with a container. |

## Before You Install

You will need:

- Permission to install software on your computer.
- An internet connection for the installer and the first image download.
- Enough disk space for Docker Desktop and downloaded images.

On a university-managed computer, installation may be restricted. Contact campus IT if you do not have permission to install or run virtualization software.

## Install Docker Desktop

Use Docker's official installation page:

- [Docker Desktop download and overview](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/introduction/get-docker-desktop/)
- [Mac installation instructions](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/mac-install/)
- [Windows installation instructions](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/)
- [Linux installation instructions](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/linux/)

### Mac

1. Download the installer for your Mac. Apple silicon Macs use the Apple silicon download; older Intel Macs use the Intel download.
2. Open the downloaded `Docker.dmg` file.
3. Drag Docker to the Applications folder.
4. Open Docker from Applications and follow the first-run instructions.
5. Wait until Docker Desktop reports that Docker is running.

### Windows

1. Download and run `Docker Desktop Installer.exe`.
2. For most students, use the recommended per-user installation.
3. Keep the WSL 2 option selected when the installer offers it, unless your IT department provides different instructions.
4. Finish the installation and restart Windows if requested.
5. Open Docker Desktop and wait until Docker is running.

## Windows: Virtualization Support Not Detected

If Docker Desktop displays **“Virtualization support not detected”**, Docker cannot access the hardware or Windows virtualization features it needs to run Linux containers. This is a Windows computer configuration issue, not an R issue.

### 1. Check whether virtualization is enabled

1. Press `Ctrl + Shift + Esc` to open **Task Manager**.
2. Select **Performance > CPU**.
3. Look for **Virtualization**.

It should say **Enabled**. If it says **Disabled**, restart the computer and open the BIOS/UEFI setup screen. Enable the setting named something like **Intel VT-x**, **Intel Virtualization Technology**, **AMD-V**, or **SVM Mode**. The name and steps depend on the computer manufacturer.

If the computer belongs to your school or employer and BIOS/UEFI settings are locked, contact IT. Do not change firmware settings unless you are comfortable doing so.

### 2. Install or update WSL 2

Open **PowerShell as Administrator** and run:

```powershell
wsl --install
wsl --update
wsl --set-default-version 2
```

Restart Windows if prompted. On supported versions of Windows, `wsl --install` enables the Windows Subsystem for Linux and Virtual Machine Platform features and installs a default Linux distribution.

Check the result with:

```powershell
wsl --status
wsl --version
```

If WSL is already installed, `wsl --update` may be all that is needed.

### 3. Check Windows features manually

If WSL installation does not work, open **Turn Windows features on or off** and make sure these features are selected:

- **Virtual Machine Platform**
- **Windows Subsystem for Linux**

Restart Windows after making changes. If Docker is configured to use Hyper-V instead of WSL 2, the required Hyper-V features must also be enabled.

### 4. Start Docker with the WSL 2 backend

After restarting:

1. Open Docker Desktop.
2. Open **Settings > General**.
3. Select **Use the WSL 2 based engine**, if that option is available.
4. Select **Apply** and restart Docker Desktop.

Docker recommends WSL 2 for most Windows installations. See [Docker's WSL 2 instructions](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/wsl/) and [Microsoft's WSL installation guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) for current requirements.

### 5. If the computer is itself a virtual machine

If Windows is running inside VMware, VirtualBox, a university virtual desktop, or another virtual machine, the host must allow **nested virtualization**. You may not be able to enable this yourself. Contact the administrator of the virtual machine or campus IT.

For additional checks, run:

```powershell
systeminfo
```

Look near the bottom for the Hyper-V requirements. Docker's [Windows installation requirements](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/) and [troubleshooting guide](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/troubleshoot-and-support/troubleshoot/topics/) describe the supported hardware and virtualization settings.

### Linux

Docker Desktop is available for some Linux distributions, but the installation steps depend on the distribution. Follow Docker's current Linux instructions rather than copying commands for a different distribution.

## First-Time Setup

When Docker Desktop opens:

1. Accept the terms when prompted.
2. Sign in only if your course or organization requires it.
3. Leave the default resource settings unless you have a reason to change them.
4. If Docker reports that a project folder cannot be mounted, open **Settings > Resources > File sharing** and share only the folder you need.

Do not share your entire home directory unless you understand the privacy and security implications. Docker's [settings documentation](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/) explains resource and file-sharing options.

## Verify the Installation

Open Terminal on Mac/Linux or PowerShell on Windows and run:

```bash
docker --version
docker version
```

Then run Docker's small test image:

```bash
docker run --rm hello-world
```

You should see a message explaining that the installation appears to be working. The `--rm` option removes the temporary container after it finishes.

If the command says that it cannot connect to the Docker daemon, open Docker Desktop and wait for it to finish starting.

## Run R in a Container

Docker Hub provides an official `r-base` image. The following command downloads the image if necessary and opens an interactive R session:

```bash
docker run --rm -it r-base
```

At the R prompt, try:

```r
2 + 3
version
q()
```

When R asks whether to save the workspace, answer `n`. The container is temporary, so files created inside it disappear when it is removed.

The [R Docker Official Image page](https://hub.docker.com/_/r-base/) contains the current image tags and usage examples.

## Use a Local Project Folder

To let a container read files from your current project folder, use a bind mount. In Terminal or PowerShell, first move into the folder containing your data or script, then run:

```bash
docker run --rm -it \
  -v "$(pwd)":/work \
  -w /work \
  r-base
```

Inside R, check the mounted folder:

```r
getwd()
list.files()
```

On Windows PowerShell, use `${PWD}` instead of `$(pwd)` if needed:

```powershell
docker run --rm -it -v "${PWD}:/work" -w /work r-base
```

The files stay on your computer because the local folder is mounted into the container. Changes made to those files can therefore be seen from RStudio on your computer.

## Useful Commands

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| List downloaded images | `docker image ls` |
| List running containers | `docker container ls` |
| List all containers | `docker container ls -a` |
| Stop a running container | `docker stop CONTAINER_ID` |
| Remove an unused container | `docker rm CONTAINER_ID` |
| Download an image | `docker pull r-base` |
| Show Docker help | `docker help` |

Replace `CONTAINER_ID` with the ID shown by Docker. Be careful with commands that remove images, containers, or volumes because they can delete local data.

## Common Problems

### `docker: command not found`

Docker Desktop may not be installed, or the terminal may have been open before installation. Install Docker Desktop, restart the terminal, and try again.

### Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

Start Docker Desktop and wait until it finishes loading. On Windows, also check that the WSL 2 feature is available and enabled if Docker Desktop is configured to use it.

### Mounts denied or permission errors

The folder may not be shared with Docker Desktop. Add only the project folder under **Settings > Resources > File sharing**, then try the command again.

### The R image is slow to download

The first download can take several minutes. Later runs reuse the downloaded image. Check your internet connection and available disk space.

### Packages disappear after the container closes

That is expected for a temporary container. Install packages in a Dockerfile or use a persistent image/volume when you need a repeatable project environment. Do not rely on an interactive container as your only copy of important work.

## Summary

The basic workflow is:

1. Install and start Docker Desktop.
2. Run `docker run --rm hello-world` to verify it.
3. Run `docker run --rm -it r-base` to start R.
4. Mount a project folder when the container needs access to local files.
5. Keep important scripts and data on your computer or in version control.
